extracted.intended_audience: readers of literary biography and criticism; writers and critics seeking craft insight
extracted.subtask_description: A literary-biographical essay on James Russell Lowell that embeds judgments about poetic and prose craft, revision practice, literary ethics, and authorial temperament; useful as guidance for critics and creative writers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lyrical and meditative poetic gift
rubrics_metrics.description: Lowell's gift is described as 'essentially lyrical and meditative' with a 'universal New England tendency to allegory.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefers lyric, reflective modes rather than dramatic plotting; such a temperament suits poems like 'The Cathedral' and explains strengths/limits of his poetic output.

rubrics_metrics.name: Undramatic actuation of characters
rubrics_metrics.description: He was 'wholly undramatic in the actuation of the characters which he imagined so dramatically.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing or attempting fiction, note that a strongly lyrical/musical writer may struggle to animate dramatic characters; the essay cites his unfinished novel as evidence that such work 'did not arrive anywhere.' Authors should choose forms that suit their temperament.

rubrics_metrics.name: First-draft vitality and publication practice
rubrics_metrics.description: He 'wrote his poems at a heat, and the manuscript which came... was usually the first draft, very little corrected.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Initial drafts often contain the poem's core energy; nonetheless, a writer may leave pieces in abeyance or later revise selectively. Editors should be aware that early versions may still be strong.

rubrics_metrics.name: Revision habits: change then sometimes revert
rubrics_metrics.description: 'He would often change them in revision, and then, in a second revision go back to the first version.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Revision is not strictly linear—reverting to an original line can be the right choice. Evaluate revisions against the poem's liveliness rather than assuming later is better.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sensitivity to criticism and corrective action
rubrics_metrics.description: He was 'very sensitive to criticism' and, when shown an unconscious resemblance to another poem, 'at once rewritten it upon wholly different lines.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Valuing criticism and acting on ethical concerns (e.g., unconscious echoing) is a mark of literary responsibility; being open to counsel can salvage reputation and integrity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding unconscious imitation (literary morals)
rubrics_metrics.description: Literary morals required an eye to others' rights; upon being alerted to resemblance he rewrote the poem rather than defending it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain vigilance for influences that verge on imitation; if pointed out, thorough and prompt revision is the ethical response.

rubrics_metrics.name: Delight in local color and vital language
rubrics_metrics.description: 'He keenly delighted in every native and novel turn of phrase... he would not undervalue a vital word or a notion picked up out of the road even if it had some dirt sticking to it.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authentic local detail and colloquial turns can enrich writing; value 'vital' words even when they are rough or unpolished.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appreciation for small touches of life and humor
rubrics_metrics.description: 'He was apt to be carried away by a little touch of life or humor, and to overvalue the piece in which he found it.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Small, specific touches can make a piece memorable; be aware of the temptation to overvalue a work for a single felicitous detail and balance judgment accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reverence for truth and intellectual honesty
rubrics_metrics.description: 'He had such reverence for the truth that he would not question it even in jest.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A critic or writer should prize honesty and accuracy; truthfulness in argument and portrayal is an important evaluative standard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dislike of affectation and pseudo-cynicism
rubrics_metrics.description: Lowell 'disliked some pseudo-cynical verses' and advised to 'sweat the Heine out of' the younger writer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid affected styles and ersatz cynicism; strive for authenticity of voice rather than fashionable poses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selectivity of form—write where strength lies
rubrics_metrics.description: Although urged to write a story, his strength lay elsewhere; his attempted novel 'would have been a failure' as recalled by the critic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assessors and writers should recognize a creator's natural forte (essay, lyric, criticism) and not force them into ill-suited forms; play to artistic strengths.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attentiveness to others' sensibilities and rights
rubrics_metrics.description: 'He was much more sensitive of others' rights than his own... most tenderly regardful of their sensibilities when he had imagined them.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When producing work, be considerate of subjects and fellow authors; sensitivity to ethical and personal implications of one's writing matters in evaluation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value of generous, meticulous mentorship
rubrics_metrics.description: He 'would go carefully over a poem... and criticise every turn of phrase' and was 'generous of himself' in aiding others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Close, constructive feedback—word-by-word attention—is valuable for craft development; critics and mentors should offer detailed, benevolent critique.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tact in criticism—avoid sneer and contempt
rubrics_metrics.description: 'One of the dangers of scholarship was... contempt... Lowell was almost as averse as Longfellow from contempt... he could snub... but I cannot remember ever to have heard him sneer.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effective criticism is firm but respectful; avoid contemptuous tone—snubbing may be momentary, but sneering undermines credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical business judgment and title/marketing influence
rubrics_metrics.description: He 'was not a good business man in a literary way... he submitted to others' judgment' about titles, feeling they 'took from the dignity of his work.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be conscious that publishing decisions (titles, marketing) affect reception; creators should balance artistic dignity with pragmatic publishing realities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Embrace of common life without condescension
rubrics_metrics.description: 'He kept as close to the common life as a man of his patrician instincts... he was always glad to talk [local accents] over with me.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include authentic representations of everyday life while avoiding condescension; genuine engagement with common speech and character enriches literature.
